summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the terms in the defining sums to show that both sequences vanish at every \(p+r\) with \(0\le r<p\); at \(p-1\), \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives the first value \(1\), while divisibility of central binomial coefficients leaves only \(k=(p-1)/2\) in the second sum, giving \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Hence both Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\) with constant anti-diagonal, and reversing the columns contributes \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), which remains in the first case and cancels the anti-diagonal sign in the second.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                         \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and perform all calculations below in the field
\(\mathbb F_p\). We will first establish the binomial congruences needed for the two sequences, then prove a general determinant reduction.

## 1. Binomial congruences modulo \(p\)

We repeatedly use the one-step form of Lucas' congruence:
\[
 \binom nk\equiv
 \binom{n\bmod p}{k\bmod p}
 \binom{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}{\lfloor k/p\rfloor}\pmod p.
\]
In particular, if \(0\le r,k,j<p\), then
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv \binom rk,
\qquad
\binom{p+r}{p+j}\equiv \binom rj.                 \tag{1}
\]
The first congruence includes the case \(k>r\), when both sides are zero.

We also need a congruence for central binomial coefficients. For every \(0\le t<p\),
\[
 \binom{2(p+t)}{p+t}\equiv 2\binom{2t}{t}.         \tag{2}
\]
Here is a complete verification, including the possible carry in \(2t\). If \(2t<p\), the base-\(p\) decompositions are
\[
2(p+t)=2p+2t,\qquad p+t=p+t,
\]
so Lucas' congruence gives
\[
\binom{2(p+t)}{p+t}
 \equiv \binom{2t}{t}\binom21
 =2\binom{2t}{t}.
\]
If instead \(2t\ge p\), write \(2t=p+u\), where \(0\le u<p\). In fact \(u<t\), since \(t<p\). Then
\[
2(p+t)=3p+u,
\]
and Lucas' congruence makes the left side of (2) a multiple of
\(\binom ut=0\). On the other hand, another application of Lucas gives
\[
\binom{2t}{t}=\binom{p+u}{t}\equiv \binom ut=0.
\]
Thus both sides of (2) vanish in this case, proving (2) in all cases.

For \(0\le k<p\), we have the familiar congruence
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.                       \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this follows inductively. It is true for \(k=0\). The standard recurrence
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k+1}(k+1)=\binom{p-1}{k}(p-1-k)
\]
becomes modulo \(p\)
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k+1}(k+1)
 \equiv-\binom{p-1}{k}(k+1).
\]
For \(k+1<p\), the element \(k+1\) is nonzero in \(\mathbb F_p\), so it can be canceled. This proves (3) by induction.

Finally, if
\[
 0\le k<p\quad\hbox{and}\quad p\le 2k,
\]
then
\[
 \binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.                             \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, write \(2k=p+u\). Since \(k<p\), one has \(u=2k-p<k\), and Lucas' congruence gives
\(
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv\binom uk=0
\).

## 2. Vanishing of \(a(p+r)\) for \(0\le r<p\)

Fix \(r<p\). Split the defining sum for \(a(p+r)\) into the indices
\(0\le k<p\) and the remaining indices, which can be written as
\(k=p+j\) with \(0\le j\le r\):
\[
 a(p+r)=
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
 +\sum_{j=0}^{r}(-1)^{p+j}\binom{p+r}{p+j}^4.
\]
By (1), the first sum is congruent to
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom rk^4.
\]
Terms with \(k>r\) are zero, so this is just
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^k\binom rk^4.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \((-1)^{p+j}=-(-1)^j\), and the second congruence in (1) shows that the second sum is
\[
 -\sum_{j=0}^{r}(-1)^j\binom rj^4.
\]
The two sums cancel. Hence
\[
 a(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(0\le r<p).             \tag{5}
\]

## 3. Vanishing of \(c(p+r)\) for \(0\le r<p\)

Again fix \(r<p\) and split the sum at \(p\). First consider an index
\(0\le k<p\). If \(k\le r\), then
\[
p+r-k=p+(r-k).
\]
Using (1) for \(\binom{p+r}{k}\) and (2) for the last central binomial coefficient gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^2\binom{2k}{k}
             \binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}\\
&\qquad\equiv
2(-1)^k\binom rk^2\binom{2k}{k}
             \binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}.                  \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(r<k<p\), then \(\binom rk=0\), while (1) also gives
\(\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk=0\). Thus (6), interpreted with a zero right side, remains valid for every \(0\le k<p\). Consequently the contribution from this first block is
\[
2\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^k\binom rk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                    \binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}=2c(r).      \tag{7}
\]

For the second block write the index as \(p+j\), where \(0\le j\le r\). Then
\[
p+r-(p+j)=r-j.
\]
By (1), (2), and the oddness of \(p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^{p+j}\binom{p+r}{p+j}^2
 \binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}\binom{2(r-j)}{r-j}\\
&\qquad\equiv
-2(-1)^j\binom rj^2\binom{2j}{j}
                     \binom{2(r-j)}{r-j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus this block contributes \(-2c(r)\), canceling (7). We conclude that
\[
 c(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(0\le r<p).             \tag{8}
\]

## 4. The values at \(p-1\)

Using (3), we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k((-1)^k)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are an odd number \(p\) of terms in the last alternating sum, beginning and ending with \(1\), so its value is \(1\). Therefore
\[
 a(p-1)\equiv1\pmod p.                             \tag{9}
\]

Now write
\[
p=2m+1,
\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
We evaluate \(c(p-1)\). We claim that all terms except the one with \(k=m\) vanish modulo \(p\). If \(k>m\), then \(p\le2k\) and \(k<p\), so (4) gives
\(
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0
\).
If \(k<m\), put \(q=p-1-k=2m-k\). Then \(q<p\), while
\[
2q=2(p-1-k)\ge p;
\]
indeed this is immediate from \(k<m\) and \(p=2m+1\). Hence (4) gives
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=\binom{2q}{q}\equiv0.
\]
Thus only \(k=m\) survives. Since \(p-1-m=m\) and \(2m=p-1\), its value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv(-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^2
             \binom{p-1}{m}\binom{p-1}{m}\\
&=(-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^4\\
&\equiv(-1)^m((-1)^m)^4=(-1)^m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.                \tag{10}
\]

## 5. An anti-triangular determinant formula

Let \(R\) be any commutative ring, and let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<n}\) be an \(n\times n\) matrix satisfying
\[
 M_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }i+j\ge n.            \tag{11}
\]
Reverse the order of the columns, forming
\[
 B_{ij}=M_{i,n-1-j}.
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
i+(n-1-j)\ge n,
\]
so (11) shows that \(B_{ij}=0\). Thus \(B\) is upper triangular, and
\[
 \det B=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}M_{i,n-1-i}.              \tag{12}
\]

The reversal permutation has sign
\[
(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}=(-1)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.         \tag{13}
\]
The first expression follows because every pair of positions is an inversion. To see the second equality, it suffices to compare parity: for \(n=2q\),
\(n(n-1)/2=q(2q-1)\) has the parity of \(q\), and for
\(n=2q+1\), \(n(n-1)/2=q(2q+1)\) again has the parity of \(q\).
Reversing the columns multiplies a determinant by this sign. Since this sign is its own inverse, (12) yields
\[
 \det M=(-1)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}
          \prod_{i=0}^{n-1}M_{i,n-1-i}.            \tag{14}
\]

We apply this to a general Hankel matrix modulo \(p\). Let
\(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z\) have the property
\[
 f(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(0\le r<p),             \tag{15}
\]
and let
\[
H_f=(f(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
If \(i+j\ge p\), then because \(i,j<p\), we can write
\[
i+j=p+r\quad\text{with }0\le r<p.
\]
Thus (15) says that, after reducing entries modulo \(p\), the matrix satisfies the anti-triangular condition (11). Every entry on its anti-diagonal is
\[
f(i+(p-1-i))=f(p-1).
\]
Formula (14), now in \(\mathbb F_p\), therefore gives
\[
 \det H_f\equiv
 (-1)^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor}f(p-1)^p.                \tag{16}
\]
For odd \(p\),
\(
\lfloor p/2\rfloor=(p-1)/2
\), and every element \(x\in\mathbb F_p\) satisfies \(x^p=x\). Hence (16) simplifies to the general reduction
\[
 \det H_f\equiv
 (-1)^{(p-1)/2}f(p-1)\pmod p.                      \tag{17}
\]

## 6. The two determinants

Take \(f=a\). Its required vanishing property is (5), and its boundary value is (9). Formula (17) gives
\[
\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
 \equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}a(p-1)
 \equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]

Next take \(f=c\). Its vanishing property is (8), and (10) gives its boundary value. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
&\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}c(p-1)\\
&\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}(-1)^{(p-1)/2}=1\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves both asserted determinant congruences.
